Conclusion Once regarded as immunologically distinct disorders, AD and AA are now understood to share convergent inflammatory pathways — centrally, JAK-STAT dependent cytokine dysregulation and Treg insufficiency/dysfunction — that together explain both their epidemiologic association and their emerging therapeutic overlap. There are several important limitations of the current evidence base. Much of the data supporting shared mechanisms derives from transcriptomic data. Agents effective in one disease may not adequately address the full pathogenic architecture of the other. Critically, the shared mechanism framework appears most robust for the atopic-associated AA endotype, wherein T h 2 dysregulation plays a prominent pathogenic role, and less so for non-atopic AA, which is characterized by predominantly T h 1-skewed inflammation. As the field advances, endotype-stratified approaches, selecting therapies based on atopic background, serum IgE, and transcriptomic immune signatures, represent the most promising path toward personalized, potentially disease-modifying interventions for both AA and AD. Continued advances in our understanding of hair follicle immune privilege, T-cell dysregulation, and type 1 and type 2 immune circuits are rapidly reshaping the treatment landscape. Emerging shared therapeutic strategies, ranging from JAK inhibitors to OX40/OX40L blockade and IL-2–modulating compounds, point toward a future in which interventions are not merely immunosuppressive but restore immune homeostasis and potentially modify disease course.

documents.title: BAD guidelines management of chronic pruritus

chunks.content: Key Summary Points Introduction Chronic pruritus (CP; lasting ≥ 6 weeks), with a prevalence of 16.8% in the working population, can occur in the context of various underlying diseases, including dermatological (e.g. atopic dermatitis, AD) and systemic conditions, such as chronic liver diseases (CLD) and chronic kidney diseases (CKD) [ ]. The prevalence of CP in CLD, particularly in cholestatic conditions such as primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), ranges from 20% to 70% [ ], and in CKD from 20% to 50% [ , ]. CP has profound physical, psychological and emotional effects, often leading to sleep disturbances, depression and anxiety. The impact on quality of life (QoL) is substantial, affecting daily functioning, social interactions and overall well-being [ , ]. Moreover, CP imposes a significant socioeconomic burden, with an individual lifetime cost estimated at $274,921 and a societal burden of $88.8 billion, driven by reduced quality-adjusted life years, healthcare expenditures and productivity losses [ ]. Different therapies are recommended depending on the cause of CP [ ]. In patients ≥ 18 years with moderate-to-severe AD, four biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab, lebrikizumab, nemolizumab) and three Janus kinase inhibitors (baricitinib, upadacitinib, abrocitinib) are currently approved according to European Medicines Agency (EMA) authorization [ ]. Pharmacological interventions for CP associated with CLD comprise cholestyramine, rifampicin, bezafibrate, gabapentinoids, opioid modulators like naloxone/naltrexone, ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors like sertraline [ , ]. Therapies for CP associated with CKD comprise difelikefalin, gabapentin, pregabalin, naloxone/naltrexone, narrowband ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation and capsaicin for localized forms [ , ]. In early-phase trials, nemolizumab reduced CP associated with CKD [ ]. In addition to pharmacological interventions, psychological therapies, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), relaxation training and mindfulness-based interventions, may be beneficial for patients with CP across all aetiologies. This is particularly important given the bidirectional relationship between CP and psychological comorbidities like anxiety and depression. Such findings highlight the role of holistic, multimodal treatment strategies that integrate both somatic and psychological care to address the complex burden of CP [ – ]. Despite the increasing number of clinical trials and the approval of promising therapies for CP in patients with CLD and CKD, there is a lack of knowledge about their specific needs and treatment goals. However, these are important for healthcare providers to adopt a patient-centred approach to CP and evaluate the treatment benefits throughout the course of the disease [ ]. The German Center for Health Services Research in Dermatology (CVderm) developed the Patient Benefit Index (PBI), a routinely used questionnaire in dermatology to assess treatment goals and evaluate the therapeutic benefit in patients with skin diseases and CP (version PBI-P) [ ]. However, instruments to assess patients’ needs and treatment goals are not routinely used by other medical specialties, such as internists or general practitioners, who typically treat patients with CP due to CLD or CKD [ ]. Therefore, our primary objective was to analyse and compare patient-reported outcomes (PRO), including disease duration, pruritus intensity, impairment of health-related QoL, psychological distress (levels of anxiety and depression), needs and treatment goals of patients with CP with associated CLD or CKD. The secondary objective was to compare these PRO to those of patients with CP and AD as a well-studied model of skin disease. The tertiary objective was to examine whether the disease burden of patients with CP (average and worst pruritus of the preceding 24 h, QoL impairment, anxiety and depression levels) impacts treatment goals. Methods Study Design and Setting A retrospective cohort study was conducted utilizing anonymized electronic health records (EHRs) from the web-based patient database of the Center for Chronic Pruritus (KCP) in Münster, Germany, which comprises data from more than 15,000 individuals. Data are collected prospectively by physicians and patients. Physicians categorize CP aetiology according to the CP classification of the International Study for the Study of Itch (IFSI) [ ] (e.g. AD, CP associated with CLD or CKD). The database systematically compiles routine clinical information, including socio-demographic characteristics, medical history, clinical manifestations, pruritus-specific parameters, PRO related to QoL, measures of anxiety and depression, as well as therapeutic needs and treatment outcomes. The EHRs analysed for this study have been routinely collected between March 1, 2012 and December 9, 2024. Study Population EHRs from all patients ( n = 2043) with the diagnostic codes “AD” ( n = 1634 patients), “CP associated with CLD” ( n = 209 patients) and “CP associated with CKD” ( n = 200 patients) were exported by experienced data managers on December 9, 2024. The data cleaning process involved systematically excluding incomplete records (especially missing information on sex, and PRO) and entries containing inconsistent or erroneous information. Subsequently, the remaining data were matched by age and sex to limit bias and ensure comparability between patients with CP with

March 1, 2012 and December 9, 2024. Study Population EHRs from all patients ( n = 2043) with the diagnostic codes “AD” ( n = 1634 patients), “CP associated with CLD” ( n = 209 patients) and “CP associated with CKD” ( n = 200 patients) were exported by experienced data managers on December 9, 2024. The data cleaning process involved systematically excluding incomplete records (especially missing information on sex, and PRO) and entries containing inconsistent or erroneous information. Subsequently, the remaining data were matched by age and sex to limit bias and ensure comparability between patients with CP with matched pairs of CLD and AD, CKD and AD, and CKD and CLD, which ultimately led to three matched sub-cohorts that could be analysed (Fig. ). Patients’ Needs and Treatment Goals We used the Patient Needs Questionnaire (PNQ), a component of the PBI-P, to assess patients’ needs and treatment goals [ ]. The PNQ consists of 27 items addressing treatment goals, each rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (“not important at all” or “not applicable”) to 4 (“highly important”). The assessed needs span multiple life domains, including physical symptoms, psychological well-being, social functioning, daily functionality and confidence in the therapy [ ]. Responses indicating “does not apply to me” were categorized as missing values in the subsequent statistical analyses and the graphical presentation, thereby excluding such items from the quantitative evaluation of patient priorities. Disease Burden The duration of illness, as stated by the patient, was analysed. Pruritus intensity was assessed using Numerical Rating Scales (NRS). Patients were asked to rate the average (AP-NRS) and worst pruritus (WP-NRS) experienced over the past 24 h (range 0–10; 0 = no, < 3 = mild, 3–6 = moderate, 7–8 = severe, 9–10 = very severe pruritus) [ ]. QoL was assessed using two validated instruments: the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and the ItchyQoL. The DLQI, with a score range of 0 to 30, consists of 10 items rated on a four-point Likert scale (0 = not at all, 1 = a little, 2 = a lot, 3 = very much) to evaluate the impact of skin diseases on patients’ lives over the past week (total range 0–30; 0–1 = no, 2–5 = small, 6–10 = moderate, 11–20 = very large, 21–30 = extremely large effect) [ ]. In contrast, the ItchyQoL, designed specifically for pruritus-related QoL assessments, includes 22 items covering three key domains (symptoms, functioning and emotions) with responses scored on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). The ItchyQoL provides a total score ranging from 22 to 110, capturing the multidimensional burden of CP [ ]. Psychological symptoms of anxiety and depression were evaluated using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), a validated self-assessment tool comprising two distinct subscales: anxiety (HADS-A) and depression (HADS-D). Each item within the scale is scored on a four-point Likert scale (0–3), resulting in subscale scores ranging from 0 to 21. Interpretation of these scores categorizes patients as follows: 0–7 indicates normal levels, 8–10 suggests potential anxiety or depression, and 11–21 reflects clinically significant anxiety or depression [ ]. Statistical Analysis Descriptive analyses were performed to characterize the study population, with categorical variables presented as frequencies and continuous variables reported as mean ± standard deviations. As a result of the exploratory study design, group comparisons used unpaired two-sample t tests (continuous variables) and chi-square tests (categorical variables). Bonferroni correction was applied to adjust for multiple testing in these correlation analyses ( α adj = 0.05/10 = 0.005). Results with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Spearman’s correlation analyses examined associations between patient-identified treatment needs (assessed with PNQ) and markers of disease burden, including pruritus intensity, QoL scores and anxiety/depression levels. Bonferroni correction was applied to adjust for multiple testing in these correlation analyses ( α adj = 0.05/6 ≈ 0.0083). All analyses were performed using R statistical software (version 4.4.1). Ethical Approval The Ethics Committee of the State Medical Association of Westfalen-Lippe, Münster, Germany approved the study (reference number 2007-413-f-S). All participants provided written informed consent prior to their inclusion in the research. Results Participants The study comprised three matched sub-cohorts (Fig. ). Sub-cohort 1 (C1) included 183 patients each with AD or CLD, with 58.5% female in both groups. Patients with CLD were significantly older than patients with AD (mean age 57.2 ± 17.4 years vs. 52.3 ± 17.4 years; p < 0.01), though patients with AD reported a longer disease duration (164.5 ± 199.2 months vs. 57.4 ± 72.6 months; p < 0.001). Sub-cohort 2 (C2) consisted of 194 matched patient pairs with AD and CKD (38.1% female each), with patients with CKD significantly older (69.7 ± 15.2 years vs. 64.8 ± 15.2 years; p < 0.005) and patients with AD exhibiting longer

(C1) included 183 patients each with AD or CLD, with 58.5% female in both groups. Patients with CLD were significantly older than patients with AD (mean age 57.2 ± 17.4 years vs. 52.3 ± 17.4 years; p < 0.01), though patients with AD reported a longer disease duration (164.5 ± 199.2 months vs. 57.4 ± 72.6 months; p < 0.001). Sub-cohort 2 (C2) consisted of 194 matched patient pairs with AD and CKD (38.1% female each), with patients with CKD significantly older (69.7 ± 15.2 years vs. 64.8 ± 15.2 years; p < 0.005) and patients with AD exhibiting longer disease duration (119.7 ± 193.6 months vs. 39.8 ± 57.6 months, p < 0.001). Sub-cohort 3 (C3) included 124 matched patients with CLD and patients with CKD (48.4% female each), with no significant differences in age or disease duration between groups (Table ). Disease Burden Patients with CLD (C1 and C3) reported moderate pruritus intensity (mean AP-NRS and WP-NRS), moderately impaired QoL (DLQI and ItchyQoL scores) and potential anxiety/depression (HADS-A/HADS-D scores). Patients with CKD (C2 and C3) demonstrated moderate AP-NRS but severe WP-NRS, moderately impaired QoL and elevated levels of anxiety and depression. Patients with AD (C1 and C2) exhibited moderate AP-NRS, with WP-NRS being moderate in C1 and severe in C2. Anxiety and depression levels were normal, but QoL was severely impaired (DLQI and ItchyQoL; Table ). Comparison of Patients with CLD and Patients with CKD (C3) No significant differences in demographic characteristics, PRO or treatment goals were identified (Table ; Fig. ). The three most important treatment goals in both disease groups were “to no longer experience itching”, “to find a clear diagnosis and therapy” and “to have confidence in the therapy” (Fig. ). Comparison of Patients with CLD and Patients with AD (C1) Patients with CLD had significantly higher levels of depression (HADS-D 7.2 ± 5.1 vs. 6.0 ± 4.3; p < 0.05), while patients with AD showed greater QoL impairment (DLQI 12.6 ± 7.4 vs. 10.4 ± 7.4; p < 0.05; ItchyQol 72.4 ± 18.0 vs. 65.0 ± 19.1, p < 0.01). Pruritus intensities (AP-NRS, WP-NRS) did not differ significantly. The most prioritized treatment goals for patients with CLD were “to no longer experience itching” (rated by 100% as “very/quite important”; PNQ 3.9 ± 0.3), “to no longer have a burning sensation on the skin” (PNQ 3.8 ± 0.8), “to find a clear diagnosis and therapy” (PNQ 3.7 ± 0.5), “to have confidence in the therapy” (PNQ 3.7 ± 0.7), “to be able to sleep better” (PNQ 3.7 ± 0.8) and “to be free of pain” (PNQ 3.7 ± 0.9). Patients with AD rated “to dare to show oneself more” significantly higher than patients with CLD (PNQ 2.6 ± 1.4 vs. 2.4 ± 1.4; p < 0.05; Fig. ). Comparison of Patients CKD and Patients with AD (C2) Patients with CKD exhibited significantly higher levels of anxiety (mean HADS-A 8.4 ± 5.3 vs. 7.0 ± 3.8; p < 0.05) and depression (mean HADS-D 9.5 ± 5.4 vs. 6.3 ± 4.2; p < 0.001) than patients with AD. No significant differences emerged in pruritus intensity or QoL impairment. Top treatment goals for patients with CKD included “to no longer experience itching”, “to find a clear diagnosis and therapy” and “to be able to sleep better”. No significant differences in any of the 27 treatment goals were observed between patients with AD and patients with CKD (Fig. ). Correlations of Treatment Goals and Disease Burden Significant correlations between patient needs and treatment goals (PNQ) and disease burden were observed across all sub-cohorts. QoL impairment (DLQI and ItchyQoL) and anxiety/depression levels (HADS-A and -D subscales) consistently correlated with PNQ in C1–C3 ( p < 0.001). Additionally, average pruritus intensity (AP-NRS) correlated with PNQ in C1 and C2, while worst pruritus intensity (WP-NRS) correlated with PNQ in C1 (Table ). Discussion The present study demonstrates that patients with CLD and CKD-associated CP experience similar levels of moderate-to-severe CP, elevated anxiety and depression, and moderate QoL impairment. Both disease groups did not differ significantly from each other regarding their demographic characteristics, PRO or treatment goals. In contrast, patients with AD, while also reporting moderate pruritus, had a significantly longer disease duration, were significantly younger and showed a significantly greater impairment of QoL compared to patients with CLD and patients with CKD, with normal anxiety and depression scores. In all disease groups, treatment goals centred on symptom improvement (less pruritus and burning sensations, better sleep), diagnostic and therapeutic clarity, and confidence in therapy. The treatment goals largely aligned in all sub-cohorts except for one treatment goal that was significantly more important to patients with AD than to patients with CLD (“to dare to show oneself more”). QoL impairment and levels of anxiety and depression correlated with patient needs and treatment goals across

were significantly younger and showed a significantly greater impairment of QoL compared to patients with CLD and patients with CKD, with normal anxiety and depression scores. In all disease groups, treatment goals centred on symptom improvement (less pruritus and burning sensations, better sleep), diagnostic and therapeutic clarity, and confidence in therapy. The treatment goals largely aligned in all sub-cohorts except for one treatment goal that was significantly more important to patients with AD than to patients with CLD (“to dare to show oneself more”). QoL impairment and levels of anxiety and depression correlated with patient needs and treatment goals across all sub-cohorts. Psychological distress in patients with CP with associated CLD and CKD was significantly higher than in patients with AD. This finding is consistent with literature. Anxiety affects 13–75% and depression 18–72% of patients with CLD [ , ]. Both conditions are highly prevalent among patients with CKD, often linked to fears of disease progression, dependency on medical care and reduced life expectancy [ ]. The chronic and often non-curative trajectory of CLD and CKD may contribute to these elevated psychological distress levels. Patients face ongoing uncertainty regarding their prognosis and limited treatment options for both CLD or CKD, and associated CP [ ]. Moreover, patients with CLD and CKD might exhibit a higher burden of systemic comorbidities compared to younger patients with AD which could impact anxiety and depression levels. Furthermore, older patients demonstrate elevated rates of anxiety and depression which might be attributable to biological aging processes and chronic disease stressors [ ]. As a result of the study design, it was unfortunately not possible to compare anxiety and depression levels between patients with CKD and CLD with CP and those without CP. However, the HADS-A and HADS-D scores observed in our study were slightly higher than those reported in the literature for patients who underwent liver transplantation, had liver cirrhosis or were receiving haemodialysis for renal insufficiency [ – ]. In these studies, CP was not specifically investigated. This may suggest that CP contributes to comparatively higher levels of anxiety and depression, even though pruritus intensities themselves did not differ significantly between groups. It is conceivable that qualitative aspects of CP or the cumulative increase in overall disease burden play a role in these elevated psychological symptoms, which represents an interesting question for future research. Although patients with AD exhibited less anxiety and depression than patients with CLD and patients with CKD, they reported higher QoL impairment than patients with CLD and patients with CKD. This difference may be attributed to visible skin lesions, related social stigma and longer disease courses, as AD frequently first manifests in early childhood [ , ]. The only significant difference in treatment goals between patients with AD and patients with CLD was that patients with AD placed greater importance on being able to show themselves more in public. This may be related to their younger age and the impact of visible skin lesions on self-esteem and social interactions [ ]. This finding underscores the importance of considering both the physical and psychosocial aspects of CP, particularly in patients with visible skin lesions. The most important treatment goals across all sub-cohorts were to no longer experience itching, to find a clear diagnosis and therapy, to have confidence in the therapy and to be able to sleep better. These priorities highlight the profound impact of pruritus on patients’ daily lives and well-being, and the strong desire for symptom relief and clarity regarding their condition. The consistency of these treatment goals across different aetiologies [ ] suggests that the experience of CP itself is a major driver of patient needs, rather than the underlying disease. The observed correlations between patient needs and treatment goals and measures of disease burden further support the notion that CP is a multidimensional symptom [ ]. These findings are in line with previous studies, which have shown that CP is associated with a range of psychological comorbidities, including depression, anxiety and sleep disturbances, and that these factors are closely linked to QoL [ – ]. The bidirectional relationship between pruritus and psychological distress highlights the importance of a holistic approach to patient care. Both the physical and mental health needs of patients with CP should be addressed. Given the high prevalence of anxiety and depression in patients with CLD and CKD, routine screening for mental health symptoms should be focused more when managing these patients. It is well established that depressive and anxious symptoms can exacerbate the severity of persistent somatic symptoms, such as pruritus [ ]. Therefore, addressing these psychological symptoms in this patient population is crucial not only to alleviate depression and anxiety themselves but also because their effective management may have a beneficial impact on pruritus severity. The limited availability of effective treatments for CP

health needs of patients with CP should be addressed. Given the high prevalence of anxiety and depression in patients with CLD and CKD, routine screening for mental health symptoms should be focused more when managing these patients. It is well established that depressive and anxious symptoms can exacerbate the severity of persistent somatic symptoms, such as pruritus [ ]. Therefore, addressing these psychological symptoms in this patient population is crucial not only to alleviate depression and anxiety themselves but also because their effective management may have a beneficial impact on pruritus severity. The limited availability of effective treatments for CP in these populations, compared to the rapidly expanding therapeutic options for AD [ ], further underscores the need for a multidisciplinary approach and the development of new, effective antipruritic drugs [ ]. Limitations This study is subject to several limitations, primarily due to its retrospective, single-centre design, which may limit the generalizability of the findings and does not allow for the assessment of longitudinal disease progression or treatment effects. While incomplete datasets were excluded during data cleaning to ensure high data quality, this process was conducted systematically by trained specialists, reducing the risk of selection bias. Since the data analysed were extracted from a database, it was unfortunately not possible to investigate the specific underlying conditions responsible for CP in patients with CLD and CKD, due to the lack of detailed coding (e.g. PBC or PSC). Moreover, the severity of the underlying comorbidities, and treatment regimens which might influence disease burden including anxiety and depression levels, and therapeutic goals could not be accounted for in the analysis. In addition, potential moderation or mediation effects could not be identified with the statistical methods employed. Conclusions This study highlights that CP severely impacts psychological well-being and quality of life in patients with atopic dermatitis, chronic liver disease and chronic kidney disease. Supplemental psychological interventions (e.g. stress coping interventions) may be beneficial in reducing psychological distress and improving overall QoL and to establish a patient-centred, holistic approach [ , , , ]. Future research should aim to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying the interplay between biological and psychological factors in CP. In addition, integrated interventions should be developed and their effectiveness in improving patient well-being should be evaluated. Furthermore, patient education and clear communication regarding the diagnosis and available treatment options can help to build trust and confidence in the therapeutic relationship, which has been shown to be a key priority for patients across all aetiologies of CP.

documents.title: BAD guidelines for the management of necrotizing fasciitis

chunks.content: Introduction Necrotizing cellulitis (NC) is a rare but serious bacterial infection of the skin that can lead to tissue destruction, severe inflammation, and potential systemic spread. NC most commonly presents in patients with pre-existing conditions that compromise immunity or tissue perfusion. Common risk factors for NC include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, chronic wounds or ulcers, recent surgeries, and IV drug use, among other factors. Necrotizing fasciitis is rapidly progressive and is characterized by high morbidity and mortality rates. Common presenting symptoms include localized pain (93.8%), swelling (80.6%), and erythema (79.5%), often accompanied by systemic signs such as fever (55%) and hypotension in advanced stages. The condition carries a mortality rate ranging from 20% to 40%, with delays in diagnosis significantly increasing the risk of death [ ]. NC is most commonly caused by Clostridium spp., Group A Streptococcus , and mixed anaerobic and facultative bacterial species [ ]. It can occur through a variety of mechanisms, including a break in the skin, puncture wounds, and ischemia, which can all lead to necrosis and gangrene of the affected area. Necrotizing fasciitis can develop rapidly, often within 12-24 hours, and presents with spreading erythema, warmth, and swelling in the affected area. It progresses with blistering, bullae, and skin necrosis. It is also associated with severe pain that seems out of proportion to visible signs and quickly worsens over the following few days [ , ]. Without prompt antibiotics or surgical debridement, sepsis and death can occur in the following one to two days after symptoms. Additionally, crepitus can sometimes be heard, indicating a gas-forming bacterium such as Clostridium spp. Dark discoloration and foul-smelling discharge are also possible. Systemic symptoms such as high fever, tachycardia, chills, and hypotension may accompany local symptoms. If testing and therapy are not begun adequately, septic shock may occur, as well as rapid necrosis and toxic shock syndrome. Diagnostic tests to identify NC include imaging studies, blood tests, and tissue cultures or Gram stains. Although there is no single definitive diagnostic guideline for necrotizing fasciitis, there are recognized clinical tools and criteria to aid diagnosis. A widely used tool to aid in the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis is the Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC), which incorporates C-reactive protein levels, white blood cell count, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose levels [ ]. When used in conjunction with imaging studies and clinical evaluation, this scoring system can help identify necrotizing fasciitis in high-risk patients. Treatment includes surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and IV fluids [ , ]. NC most commonly develops following a disruption of the integumentary barrier, permitting the translocation of pathogenic microorganisms, typically polymicrobial flora including anaerobes and facultative anaerobes, into subcutaneous tissues. In high-risk ischemic regions, such as digits or extremities with compromised vascular supply, the susceptibility to infection increases significantly due to hypoperfusion. Ischemia results in diminished oxygen tension, impaired neutrophil function, and reduced delivery of essential metabolic substrates such as glucose, creating an ideal microenvironment for anaerobic bacterial proliferation. This facilitates the production of bacterial exotoxins and proteolytic enzymes. This promotes rapid tissue necrosis and fascial dissection. Additionally, ischemic tissues exhibit reduced immune surveillance and delayed wound healing, exacerbating the risk of infection. The resulting inflammatory cascade and tissue degradation can precipitate systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and sepsis. Prompt recognition and intervention, including surgical debridement, hemodynamic support, and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, are imperative to mitigate morbidity and mortality in patients [ ]. Although NC is a rare medical concern in the United States, accounting for around 1,000 cases yearly, proper management and treatment are necessary to prevent significant necrosis, tissue damage, and possible amputation [ ]. In accordance with the practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections by the Infectious Diseases Society of America, common medical management treatments include broad-spectrum antibiotics, targeted antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation therapies, and vasopressor support to help patients with this infection [ ]. Close and regular monitoring is needed to prevent serious symptoms in patients with NC. This case is a unique presentation of a patient who presents with severe pain in her right digit after wearing a very tight ring. This may have led to ischemia and the growth of bacteria, leading to NC. and the growth of bacteria, leading to NC. Case presentation A 62-year-old female presented to the emergency department with tissue and skin necrosis of the right ring finger. She was wearing a silver ring that had eroded through the skin of her finger (Figure ). There had been pain and swelling of the finger for five days, and she came to the emergency department when she could no longer feel or move the finger. At arrival, the patient presented with fever, weakness, and tachycardia. The initial blood pressure was 105/60 mmHg, her white blood cell count was elevated at 17,000/mm³, and serum lactate was 5.2 mmol/L. These findings were suggestive of tissue hypoxia secondary to sepsis from infection at the site of the finger wound. Blood cultures were taken, and she was promptly administered two 1000 cc bags of IV 0.9% saline as well as Zosyn (piperacillin and tazobactam) 4.5 g infused over six hours. Following this, her blood pressure increased to 120/75 and remained stable during her ED stay. Her current medication list included metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and alprazolam (Xanax). Laboratory values and vital signs are summarized in Table . On closer examination, the wound appeared ischemic and malodorous. When the ring was gently moved, bone was visible underneath. Crepitus was present on physical exam, but X-rays did not show any pockets of air (Figure ). The ring was unable to be removed in the ED, as there was no space to insert a cutting instrument. The patient was transferred to an orthopedic hand surgeon, where the ring was cut in the operating room (OR). Duplex ultrasound revealed no distal perfusion of the finger following removal of the ring, so the right ring finger was amputated at the third (distal) phalanx. Blood cultures were later positive for Streptococcus A . After three days, she was discharged home with recommendations for home nursing to manage the dressing of the wound. Discussion Ring erosion to the bone of a finger involves continuous pressure, edema, and ischemia. Prolongation of the repetitive trauma can lead to infection, cellulitis in the case of our patient, and require amputation. Previous reports and reviews have not discussed amputation of a digit as a consequence of ring embedment [ ]. Our patient presents a unique case of ring embedment that required digital amputation due to an inability to remove the ring and risk of reperfusion injury. Pressure ulcers The swelling of the finger may be secondary to pressure ulcers, which involve continuous pressure over bony prominences or constricted areas, which can lead to the disruption of local blood flow [ ]. As seen in this case, this can lead to ischemia and necrosis of the localized soft skin and tissue [ ]. Such ischemia can also create an anaerobic environment, providing ideal conditions for bacterial colonization and infection, as seen with the patient’s cellulitis. Evidence suggests that even mild pressure over long durations of time can induce tissue hypoxia due to capillary bed occlusion at pressures above 32 mmHg [ ]. In this case, the ring, acting as the constrictive force, allowed for the exacerbation of local ischemia and bacterial entry into the epidermis. A case report outlining the partial embedding of a ring around a finger outlines how digital swelling can be exacerbated by the presence of the ring, leading to venous congestion and, therefore, arterial compromise [ ]. In evaluating pressure ulcers, there are three risk assessment scales: Waterlow, Norton, and Braden [ - ]. The higher the score, the greater the susceptibility for an individual to experience a pressure ulcer. The Braden scale is most commonly used due to its ease and incorporation of risk factors. The Braden scale assesses pressure ulcer risk by evaluating sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear [ , ]. Our patient, presenting with diabetes, ischemic tissue, and immobility in the affected finger, was at increased risk for localized pressure ulcers and poor wound healing. The patient could not feel or move the affected finger, indicating complete sensory loss in that area. The wound was malodorous and ischemic, suggesting it was frequently moist due to infection and necrosis. The patient had diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension, which suggests potential dietary concerns affecting healing and overall nutritional status. Along with other factors of sepsis and weakness, we predict the patient to have a score of 12, placing the patient in the high-risk category for pressure ulcers. The lack of perfusion compounded the risk of tissue breakdown, emphasizing the importance of early intervention and pressure offloading strategies. In future practice, incorporating Braden scale assessments in similar cases can help predict and mitigate pressure-related complications. dietary concerns affecting healing and overall nutritional status. Along with other factors of sepsis and weakness, we predict the patient to have a score of 12, placing the patient in the high-risk category for pressure ulcers. The lack of perfusion compounded the risk of tissue breakdown, emphasizing the importance of early intervention and pressure offloading strategies. In future practice, incorporating Braden scale assessments in similar cases can help predict and mitigate pressure-related complications. Ischemia Oxygen is an essential factor in tissue repair and infection control. Hypoxia is often seen in infected tissues and can impair neutrophil function, therefore reducing effective bacterial clearance and delaying wound healing [ ]. A combination of compromised oxygenation due to a loss of local blood flow from mechanical pressure and infection-based inflammation likely reflects the lack of perfusion in this patient’s presentation. Evidence suggests that hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is an innovative approach to enhance wound healing in the case of severe infection management. HBOT is a technique that increases oxygen solubility in plasma, thereby promoting collagen synthesis, angiogenesis, and bacterial killing by neutrophils [ ]. In terms of microbial infections, evidence suggests that HBOT can be considered for non-healing wounds in an attempt to break bacterial biofilms [ ]. Yet, the most important application of antimicrobial activity for HBOT can be applied to necrotizing soft tissue infections. Anaerobic bacteria are killed at a much higher rate when HBOT is used, which can decrease levels of inflammatory factors, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-10 [ ]. This can lead to improved oxygen flow and prevent the need for amputation. HBOT has also been shown to play a role in angiogenesis and revascularization with the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) [ ]. Studies show that HBOT, which is used as adjunct therapy for diabetic foot ulcers, can provide faster healing and better outcomes than patients not treated with HBOT [ ]. As wound hypoxia remains a strong risk factor for patients with non-healing wounds, increasing oxygen on a cellular level is a tactic to help upregulate growth factors, reduce inflammation, increase collagen and blood vessel synthesis, and eliminate bacteria. Studies continue to depict lower major amputation rates for diabetic foot ulcers with the use of adjunctive HBOT [ ]. Ischemia played a central role in this case, as the prolonged constriction from the ring led to necrosis. The inability to perfuse the digit after ring removal confirmed irreversible tissue damage. This highlights the need for early recognition of ischemic changes in similar cases, where prolonged vascular compromise can lead to necrotic progression. Clinically, practitioners should prioritize prompt assessment of circulation and tissue viability in patients with constrictive injuries to improve outcomes and minimize amputation risk. Vascular reperfusion injuries Post amputation, the revascularization of ischemic tissue can trigger oxidative stress and inflammatory processes, which can exacerbate cellular damage. Such reperfusion injury involves the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), microvascular vasoconstriction, and activation of neutrophils to release proinflammatory cytokines, which further damage tissue [ ]. Management of reperfusion injuries involves adequate hydration pre- and postoperatively to help maintain flow and reduce renal damage from toxic metabolites. Additionally, the use of bicarbonate or other agents can reduce acidosis that occurs during reperfusion [ ]. The prevention of vascular reperfusion injury includes ischemic pre- or post-conditioning, which involves organ exposure to small durations of ischemia and limited reperfusion of the organ in order to prevent ROS formation [ ]. Reperfusion injury was a major concern in this case, influencing the decision not to cut the ring in the emergency setting. Sudden restoration of blood flow to ischemic tissues can lead to significant oxidative stress and inflammation, exacerbating tissue damage. This case illustrates the delicate balance between timely intervention and the potential harms of reperfusion injury. Future clinical guidelines should consider risk stratification for reperfusion injury, especially in patients with chronic ischemic insults, to optimize both surgical timing and patient outcomes. Conclusions This rare case of ring-induced NC necessitating amputation underscores the need for prompt recognition of ischemic injuries. Risk assessment tools like the Braden scale may aid prevention, though HBOT's role requires further study. Clinicians should maintain a high suspicion for vascular compromise in constrictive ring injuries to avert irreversible damage.

documents.title: BAD guidelines for management of chronic urticaria

chunks.content: Real life management of chronic urticaria: Multicenter and cross sectional study on patients and dermatologists in Iran. Recently, advances in understanding the etiology of urticaria and updates of diagnostic and therapeutic management guidelines have drawn attention to chronic urticaria (CU) morbidity. The present study aimed to evaluate Iranian dermatologists' practice and real life management of CU patients. A total of 35 dermatologists and 443 patients were included in the study. Number of female patients was 321 (72.5%). Mean (standard deviation) age of the study patients was 38 (13) years and the median (inter quartile range) of disease duration was 12 (6-48) months. Severity of patients' symptoms was mild for 32.1%, moderate for 38.7%, severe for 18.8%, and 10.4% of them had no evident signs or symptoms. The most common diagnostic methods were physical examination (96.6%), differential blood count (83.5%), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (77.4%), and C-reactive protein (62.8%). The number of dermatologists prescribed nonsedating antihistamines (nsAH) in regular dose and high dose mono therapy were 26 (74%) and 6 (17%), respectively. About 66% of dermatologists were familiar with British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) guideline. The most common first-line treatment for CU by Iranian dermatologists was nonsedating antihistamines in regular or high doses. The real-life management of patients with CU in Iran was in accordance with the available practice guidelines.
